formats.name: Number hook (kept, made specific)
formats.structure: 1) Lead with one verifiable figure from the article, with its unit, time frame and source, for example '[figure] of [defined group] did [specific thing], according to [named dataset]'. 2) In the second line, say what the number means and what the article does with it. Keep the post to about 100-200 characters of setup. 3) Add a chart or image if you can. 4) Put the article link in the first reply with a one-line description, such as 'Full methodology and breakdown here'. Roundup posts say X's open-source code has no hard link penalty, and Musk said in July that link posts aren't penalised. However, other creator tests still report weaker reach for link-in-body posts. Treat link-in-reply as the safe default and A/B test it against link-in-body. 5) Don't use a number the article doesn't state outright. Specificity is the trust signal.
formats.example: Women hold [exact share] of senior roles in [defined sector], and the gap is widest at [specific level]. We broke down the data by company size. Source and method in the reply below.

formats.name: Buried detail, 'what the report says on page X' (kept)
formats.structure: 1) Name the report or filing type and the page or section where the finding sits, for example 'On page [X] of the [report type]...'. 2) State the detail plainly in one sentence. Do not tease it. 3) Add one line of context on why it matters or what it contradicts. 4) Attach a screenshot of the highlighted passage as the native proof. 5) Put the link in the first reply: 'Our full read of the report'. Because the source is shown, this format builds credibility and doesn't need clickbait. The article should give more than the post does, such as analysis, comparison and context.
formats.example: Page [X] of a new report on women-led businesses has a finding the executive summary leaves out: [plain statement of the finding]. Screenshot below. Our analysis of what it changes is in the reply.

formats.name: Myth vs data, the one-two reversal (kept)
formats.structure: 1) Post 1 states the common belief fairly, as a claim people actually make, not a strawman. 2) Post 2, or the second half of the same post, gives the data point that complicates it, with its source. 3) Add a single line that says what the data does not prove. This keeps it credible and avoids over-claiming. 4) Invite replies with a pointed question, such as 'Does this match what you see in your sector?'. Replies carry far more ranking weight than likes. Then answer replies quickly, because author replies are reported as a strong signal. 5) Link the full piece in the first reply. Contrarian and data-led hooks outperformed generic advice hooks in one Threads analysis, so test the same pattern on X before relying on it.
formats.example:
The belief: women-founded businesses struggle because they don't ask for funding.

What the data shows: [specific finding on application rates versus approval rates]. It doesn't show why, and the article looks at the three explanations researchers offer. Full piece in the reply.

formats.name: Open question with the answer in the thread (kept)
formats.structure: 1) Ask one narrow, answerable question the article actually resolves, such as 'Which [type] of firm closed the pay gap fastest?'. Avoid broad prompts like 'Thoughts?'. 2) In the same post, say the answer is in the thread. 3) Reply 1 gives the direct answer in a sentence. Don't make people wait for it. 4) Reply 2 gives the evidence, and reply 3 gives the caveat. 5) Put the article link in the last reply as 'The full breakdown'. 6) Respond to the first replies within 30 minutes. Early engagement and replies matter most for reach, according to several 2026 guides. The question must be one the article really answers.
formats.example: Which type of company has done most to widen the pipeline of women into senior management, and which has done least? We checked the evidence. Answer and caveats in the thread below.

formats.name: One chart, one takeaway (kept, spreading)
formats.structure: 1) Make one clean chart with a single message and a headline that states the finding, not just the topic. 2) Label the source, date and unit directly on the image. 3) Write one sentence of takeaway above it, in plain language. 4) Add alt text with the finding. 5) Reply with the link and one sentence on what else the article covers, such as other cuts of the data or expert reaction. 6) Say if the chart is simplified. 7) Don't truncate axes in ways that exaggerate. Several 2026 guides list data visualisations among the top impression drivers on X. In Buffer's analysis, images nearly matched text for median engagement, at 3.40% against 3.56%. Treat these as directional, because sample sizes and methods differ between studies.
formats.example: One chart: [metric] for women-led firms versus the sector average, [year range]. The takeaway: the gap narrows at [stage] and reopens at [stage]. Source is on the chart. Our analysis of why is in the reply.

formats.name: Native long-post excerpt (new, replaces the swipe card post)
formats.structure: 1) If your account has Premium, use a long-form post of about 300-1,500 words that delivers the article's single strongest finding natively. Open with a standalone first line, because only the opening shows before 'Show more'. 2) Give the key finding, the evidence, the caveat and a short 'what to watch next'. 3) Close with 'The full reporting, data and interviews are here' and put the link in the post or in the first reply. 4) Don't hold back the core answer, because the post earns attention before it asks for the click. The reason for the swap is that the evidence that swipe or carousel formats work comes mostly from LinkedIn and Instagram, not X. Native long text and images fit X's text-first behaviour better. One teardown also found Articles averaged about 10x the views of creators' regular posts. That sample was only 13 creators, and it's a vendor study, so test it on your own account.
formats.example:
Opening line: What [new survey/report] actually found about women moving from mid-level to senior roles.

Then: three short findings with sources, one caveat about what the data can't show, and a closing line pointing to the full analysis.

formats.name: Short proof thread, 3-6 posts (kept)
formats.structure: 1) Post 1 makes one claim, stated honestly, with the strongest evidence. Don't promise anything the thread doesn't deliver. 2) Each following post has one sourced fact, quote or chart, and works on its own. 3) The final-but-one post gives the limitation or counter-evidence. 4) The last post says 'The full piece covers [two specific things not in this thread]' and links the article. Alternatively, put the link in reply 2 and repeat it at the end. 5) Keep it to 3-6 posts. Analyses report threads at the top of engagement rates, at 1.89% in one 87,528-post dataset. One vendor guide suggests that completion drops sharply after about 12 posts, so shorter is safer. Our 3-6 range also protects completion.
formats.example:
1/ Our reporting found that [claim about women in business], and here's the evidence.
2/ [Sourced fact].
3/ [Chart or quote].
4/ What this doesn't show: [limitation].
5/ The full analysis, including [two specifics], is here: [link]

formats.name: Breaking-style 'what we know' update (kept, tightened)
formats.structure: 1) Start with a plain label and the confirmed fact in one line, such as 'Developing: [what happened]'. 2) Use three short blocks: Confirmed (with named sources), Not yet confirmed, and What's next, with a time if you know it. 3) Don't use 'BREAKING' on stories that aren't. 4) Add a timestamp. 5) Reply to this same post with updates, instead of posting new standalone updates. This keeps the post's engagement together and builds the reply signal. 6) Link the live article in the first reply and say it's being updated. Community Notes are now reported to demote reach on posts that get them, so accuracy and clear sourcing matter for distribution as well as for brand credibility.
formats.example:
Developing: [confirmed event involving a women-led business or policy].

Confirmed: [fact and source].
Not yet confirmed: [open point].
Next: [expected announcement or time].

We're updating this thread, and our live article is in the reply.
